book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_

chapters.relation: Louis Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's 'blind squirrel' lie about Earth, classifying the fact that Cylons look human, Roslin's faked death of the baby Hera, and Tom Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. Democratic duty is framed as a deontological obligation of transparency grounded in the governed's trust, while the leadership repeatedly defaults to consequentialist wartime exceptions. The chapter proposes a rule-of-thumb: secrecy is justified only to hide specific information from an external threat like the Cylons, never to protect the government from its own citizens, and each violation erodes the trust on which Colonial democracy's 'soul' depends.

chapters.file: ch31 - Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t.md
chapters.relation: Bryan McHenry asks whether manipulating religious belief for political ends is ever moral, using Adama's motivational lie about Earth, Roslin's Pythia-driven 'dying leader' campaign (compared with George W. Bush's faith-based politics), and the Cylons' evangelical monotheism aimed at scaring Baltar into conversion. Machiavelli's Prince licenses rulers who use a religion they do not share, and the chapter judges Adama's hope-based use of the Earth myth and Roslin's uniting religiosity as essentially moral while the Cylons wield faith as a coercive weapon. Madison's Enlightenment demand that religion be directed by reason and conviction rather than force supplies the standard the fear-based Cylon conversion of Baltar fails.

John Kenneth Muir argues the 1978 original series was serious Cold War allegory, not the 'popcorn' Ron Moore dismissed: President Adar's armistice with the Cylons mirrors Carter-era detente and the SALT treaties, Adama's 'preparedness' embodies the American Security Council's 'Peace through Strength' doctrine, and Sire Uri's disarmament bid plays the naive appeaser. In 'Experiment in Terra' Apollo delivers a Goldwater-Reagan-style speech to a Western Alliance menaced by an Eastern Bloc surrogate whose sneak nuclear attack vindicates him. The chapter concludes the original's moral absolutism was genuine political commentary, just as serious as the re-imagined series' post-9/11 allegory.

chapters.file: ch33 - MODEL FIVE - Finding Purpose in the Void.md

chapters.relation: Jean-Paul Martinon reads the episode '33', where the fleet jumps every thirty-three minutes for over 130 hours, as a study in a temporality 'of the limit': an interrupted life sandwiched between the death of the Colonies and death at Cylon hands. The survivors' existence becomes eschatological and 'bare' (following Agamben), stripped of history and future with death as the only horizon, and the FTL jump becomes a metaphor for Derrida's messianic to-come, the sliver of undecidable hope between promise and danger. Baltar's line that the universe is a serendipitous system versus Number Six's 'God is watching out for you' marks the fatality-contingency undecidability that structures Colonial time.

Trudy Milburn applies Dewey's account of habit, impulse and inquiry to navigation in the series: Adama's 'I know the way to Earth' declaration starts an inquiry whose end-in-view is continuously reformulated as humans creatively combine scriptures, pulsars and constellations as signs. Roslin uses scripture at face value and other people's belief in it, which on Dewey's anti-foundationalist terms is legitimate map-making rather than piety. The Cylons, by contrast, treat their plan as God-given, cannot reinterpret signs for themselves (needing Baltar to locate Earth) and fall back on inherited habit, which is why, on Dewey's view, they are the ones who are lost.

chapters.file: ch36 - Free to Be You and Me.md
chapters.relation: Bryan Barker reconciles Cylon programming and human 'destiny' with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's intelligible character: Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama under activation, Baltar's cowardly conversion to the Cylon God, Tigh's decision to stay at his post upon learning he is a Cylon, and Starbuck's flight into the storm in 'Maelstrom' all express innate, unchanging character rather than external compulsion. Even destiny, as in Leoben's prophecies to Starbuck, works like determinism unless reframed as character. On this view we are free because everything we do manifests who we immutably are, whether that character is programmed or born.

chapters.file: ch37 - Taking in the View from the Paranoid Position.md
chapters.relation: Psychoanalyst Christopher Christian reads the series through Freud's death instinct and Melanie Klein's paranoid position: Starbuck's recklessness, Tigh's alcoholism and poisoning of Ellen, and Apollo's and Starbuck's peaceful death-hallucinations fuse Eros and Thanatos, while the Chief's sleepwalking attack on Cally shows the death drive deflected outward as aggression. Because humans project their own destructiveness onto the Cylons ('toasters', 'it'), they must keep the machines perpetually in view, leaving the whole fleet stuck in Klein's paranoid position. Cain's torture of Gina in Razor thus becomes a splitting operation meant to keep evil safely outside the self.

David Vessey argues the humanoid Cylons' resurrection denies them the 'successful death' that makes a life meaningful: like Greek heroes governed by moira or Socrates drinking the hemlock, mortals must be able to see life as a completed whole that death can crown, with how one lived shaping what death means. Cylon deaths (dying out of range of a resurrection ship, D'Anna being boxed) are always failures or shames, and their religion carries no after-death stakes, unlike Socrates' philosophical preparation for death. Camus's Sisyphus shows agency and the option of suicide remain necessary for meaning, while Plato's Symposium model of immortality through children is the only one left to the Cylons, via mortal human-Cylon babies like Hera.

chapters.file: ch39 - MODEL SIX - Near the End of Our Journey.md

chapters.relation: Ivan Wolfe shows that Glen Larson's original series is 'ontologically Mormon': Kobol anagrammatizes Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve mirrors the LDS hierarchy, marriage is a 'sealing' for eternity, the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were' restates Lorenzo Snow's couplet on human deification, and Count Iblis can rule only those who freely submit, since agency is supreme in Mormon theology. Because none of this is epistemologically required viewing knowledge, later licensees could rewrite the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics became an incoherent muddle by abandoning the inviolability of free will, while Hatch's novels and Moore's re-imagining built new ontologies, Moore replacing progressive godhood with the circular 'all this has happened before.'

Richard Berger reads the 're-imagined' series through Bakhtin's dialogism: Moore's show is not a GINO remake but a polyphonic dialogue with the 1978 series and its own sources, including the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greek myth and fan fiction. That polyphony appears on screen as a spectrum of belief, from Baltar's militant atheism argued over with Number Six's fundamentalism, a staging of the Dawkins-Hitchens debate in which the two extremes prove close enough for conversion, to Roslin's prophetic politics. The chapter argues the reboot is 'more Battlestar Galactica' because it makes the original's latent religious debates explicit.

The chapter casts the two series as opposed worldviews: the original is Manichaean moral absolutism, with 'War of the Gods' staging Count Iblis and the Ships of Light as cosmic Darkness and Light battling over humanity, while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean moral relativism where context decides right and wrong. Its clearest cases are comparative: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of the fleet's fuel reserves to rescue Starbuck, and Leoben is airlocked after interrogation while the tortured Athena and Gina are treated with mercy. The fan schism between the shows, it concludes, is really the centuries-old quarrel between absolutism and relativism.

Ewan Kirkland argues BSG's gender-free surface, unisex bunks and a Starbuck who never has to defend her right to fly, masks a default masculinity under Adama's patriarchal regime: Ellen is killed off as the negative femme fatale, Kat and Cain die or turn monstrous, and 'The Farm' literalizes feminist fears of patriarchal medicine turning women into breeders. Starbuck confounds the sexualizing male gaze, never objectified, repeatedly rescuing men and reversing damsel-in-distress plots, yet her success is entirely masculinized, bought by becoming like a man. Her New Caprica captivity as Leoben's simulated wife literalizes the feminist critique of compulsory heterosexuality, and her death in 'Maelstrom', submitting to her former kidnapper, suggests the series contains its most transgressive heroine.

chapters.file: ch44 - Human, Machine, or Something In-between.md
chapters.relation: Heather Rolufs maps Boomer Sharon and Caprica Six onto Eve and Lilith: Boomer's unwitting shooting of Adama parallels Eve eating the fruit before she could understand disobedience, raising whether her free will was ever real, while Baltar repeats Adam's blame-shifting and Six gains the rebuttal Eve never had. The Lilith material from the Alphabet of Ben Sira and the Zohar explains Six's red-dressed seduction of Baltar and her ambivalent violence, snapping a baby's neck as a mercy before the attack yet later risking herself to return Hera. The chapter argues the show lets these demonized first women of myth be reread as neither machines nor demons but human.

This fan story stages the fanfiction debate inside the fleet: Roslin recites the 'Scorpion School' line, Adorno's mass culture mindlessly absorbed and Benjamin's fear that reproduction destroys an artwork's aura, while aide Billy Keikeya counters with Henry Jenkins, arguing fanfiction is culture repairing myths owned by corporations and that the zine writers build real community. Baltar, secretly a fan himself, needles Number Six by calling the Cylons 'a fanfiction of the human brain,' and her insistence that there should be one singular truth of the show mirrors her fundamentalist monotheism. Adama and Roslin conclude the fan writers are harmless, even healing, leaving creativity and communal play on the human side of the human-Cylon divide.

Using Wayne Booth's coduction, the ethical evaluation of fiction refined through open, informed conversation, this chapter argues BSG is a highly ethical show precisely because it keeps moral debate alive instead of preaching: the unresolved New Caprica suicide-bombing storyline, where an unsympathetic Baltar confronts a saintly Roslin in jail and she still cannot justify the bombings, invites the audience to do the ethical work. The chapter distinguishes Tolkien's allegory from applicability to block a one-to-one Iraq reading, and holds up Ronald Moore's candid blog exchange about the absence of gay characters as coduction in action. Sustained conversation, it concludes, is both the best defense against censorship and the best way to judge art.

chapters.file: ch54 - The Universe is a vast and complex system coincidental, serendipitous events.md

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Italian philosopher whose concept of 'bare life' names human existence stripped to mere biological survival, outside political meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 34 uses Agamben's bare life to describe the fleet's existence in '33' as survival reduced to the brink of death between jumps.

holes.name: The Messianic 'To-Come' (democratie a venir)
holes.what: Derrida's notion of an unpredictable opening onto the future, a promise that is never present but structures hope and decision.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads the fleet's FTL jumps as metaphors for Derrida's messianic to-come, the sliver of hope between promise and danger.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis who late in life posited the death instinct (Thanatos) warring against Eros, the life instinct.
holes.why: Chapter 37 makes Freud's death instinct the fulcrum of the series, reading Starbuck, Tigh and Baltar as fusing life and death drives.

holes.name: Melanie Klein
holes.what: Psychoanalyst who placed infantile aggression and the projection/splitting of badness at the center of development, source of the paranoid position.
holes.why: Chapter 37's title concept is Klein's paranoid position, into which the whole human fleet is stuck after projecting its destructiveness onto the Cylons.

holes.name: The Death Instinct (Thanatos)
holes.what: Freud's unconscious drive toward quietude, inorganic rest and self-destruction, opposed to and fused with Eros.
holes.why: Chapter 37 analyzes Starbuck's self-sabotage, Tigh's drinking and the peaceful death-hallucinations as expressions of the death drive.

holes.name: The Paranoid Position
holes.what: Klein's early-infantile stance of projecting one's own aggression into others and remaining perpetually vigilant for its return.
holes.why: Chapter 37 argues humans project all evil onto the Cylons and must keep them in sight, leaving the fleet stuck in the paranoid position.

holes.name: Mormon Theology (LDS metaphysics)
holes.what: Latter-day Saint metaphysics: Kolob, eternal progression toward godhood ('as man now is, God once was'), and absolute, inviolable moral agency.
holes.why: Chapter 40 argues the original BSG's ontology, Kobol, the Quorum of Twelve, sealing, deification and supreme free will, is built from Mormon theology.

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian theorist of the dialogic: language and texts as many-voiced (heteroglossic, polyphonic) dialogues rather than single-authored utterances.
holes.why: Chapter 41's whole case that Moore's series is a 're-imagining' in dialogic parallel, not a GINO remake, rests on Bakhtin's theory.

holes.name: Dialogism (polyphony, heteroglossia)
holes.what: Bakhtin's view that texts converse with past and future texts through many equally authoritative voices.
holes.why: Chapter 41 uses dialogism to describe how the two series, their religious and pseudo-archaeological sources, and fanfic talk to each other.

holes.name: Manichaeism (Light versus Darkness)
holes.what: Mani's third-century dualist religion: a universe split between good Light and evil Darkness warring over humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 42 reads the original series' 'War of the Gods', Count Iblis versus the Beings of Light, as dramatized Manichaean moral absolutism.

holes.name: Compulsory Heterosexuality
holes.what: Adrienne Rich's concept that heterosexuality is an imposed political institution enforced by social pressure, not a natural inevitability.
holes.why: Chapter 43 reads Starbuck's captivity as Leoben's simulated wife on New Caprica as a literalization of the feminist critique of compulsory heterosexuality.

holes.name: The Lilith Myth
holes.what: Jewish legend (Alphabet of Ben Sira, the Zohar) of Adam's first wife, created from the same earth as Adam, who left Eden and was later demonized as a child-stealing seductress.
holes.why: Chapter 44 maps Number Six and Sharon onto Eve and Lilith, arguing BSG lets the demonized first women of myth be redeemed.

holes.name: Participatory Culture (textual poaching, fan fiction)
holes.what: Henry Jenkins's account of fans who actively rewrite corporate-owned myths, creating value and community the originals lack.
holes.why: Chapter 45 is a fan story whose theme is whether fan fiction has value, pitting Jenkins against Adorno and Benjamin's culture-industry pessimism.

holes.name: Coduction (Booth's ethical criticism)
holes.what: Wayne Booth's method of judging fiction ethically through sustained, informed, open-minded conversation among readers.
holes.why: Chapter 46 uses coduction to argue BSG is ethical because it invites open moral conversation, on suicide bombing and gay characters, instead of preaching.
